title: Chapter Twenty-Nine: Yayu
bio: “Yayu” — In the Classic of Mountains and Seas (“Western Lands Within the Seas”), the yayu has a snake’s body and a human face; it was killed by the minister of Erfu. As the saying goes: the old body is dead, and a new face is only now being born.
paragraphs: The night he got back from Shanghai, Zheng Zhiyong sat in his office until the small hours.

What Wu You had said to him, he didn’t tell a soul. But all the way back from Shanghai, what kept running through his head, over and over, were scenes of Wu Peng at his side these past few months. Wu Peng bringing him noodles; Wu Peng sitting with Lu You in the lobby bar for more than an hour; Wu Peng telling him the news about Yuanwang’s funding bet; Wu Peng meeting him at the airport, carrying his suitcase, setting up times with Wu You for him. He used to think all this was just what an assistant ought to do — done carefully, done properly, done so you never had to worry. Now he knew that behind every single thing Wu Peng did, there might be a record.
Because on this business trip to Shanghai, he had discovered something — something he hadn’t seen coming at all.

The day he was waiting for Wu You in the Shanghai office, his eye fell on a pile of papers on Wu You’s desk, with Wu You’s ID card lying on top. He gave them a quick glance: a pile of board information, business-registration forms, change-of-registration documents. Zheng Zhiyong looked out the door, made sure Wu You wouldn’t be coming in any time soon, picked up his ID card and glanced at it.

At first he didn’t think anything of it; his eyes skimmed over it and he put the card down. Then, suddenly, it was as if something came back to him, and he immediately picked the card up again and went over the details on it carefully.

The home address on Wu You’s ID card looked familiar. He took a photo of the card, sat back down on the sofa beside the desk, took out his phone and scrolled through his earlier WeChat chats with Wu Peng, in which there was an ID card Wu Peng had once sent him. Baolian Road, Yanta District, Xi’an — even the character for “Room” in brackets in the house number was the same.

Zheng Zhiyong zoomed in on the screen and looked at it for a long time. He remembered Wu You saying once in passing that his family home was in Xi’an — two brothers, and the whole family had been there for several generations.
One named Wu, the other named Wu too, the same household-registration address.

Zheng Zhiyong leaned back in his chair and turned it over in his mind a few times. Wu You was just past forty, Wu Peng in his twenties, the age gap under twenty years. Father and son didn’t quite fit. That left only one possibility — uncle and nephew, blood uncle and nephew.

He remembered what Wu Peng had said when he first came to the company: “My family did happen to know Mr. Wu, so they introduced me, and I was lucky enough to get to work and learn under him.” Hearing it then, it sounded like an ordinary well-connected kid who’d gotten in through a favor. Looking at the words again now, every one of them carried weight. “My family knew him” — that was his own uncle. “They introduced me” — that was a man keeping his own nephew close.

Sitting in Wu You’s office, the more Zheng Zhiyong thought about it, the colder his back went. He remembered the things he’d said in front of Wu Peng. Drunk, saying “It took me only a few months to hit bottom and bounce back”; saying “I’m going to pin Yuanwang to the ground and pound it, beat Gao Fei till he’s hunting for his teeth on the floor”; saying “Wu You doesn’t know a damn thing, he’s always fucking sticking his nose into everything.” He’d said it all with great satisfaction at the time, and Wu Peng had sat there listening, smiling, not interrupting, not chiming in, just listening. He’d thought that was an assistant’s sense of proper bounds. Only now did he understand: it was a pair of eyes Wu You had placed beside him.

Now he was back in Xi’an, and it was still Wu Peng who’d picked him up and brought him back to the office. Seeing him there, as poised and well-mannered as ever, Old Zheng couldn’t help a lingering chill, and very politely told him to go on home and get some rest early. He remembered the time Lu You came to Xi’an, when Wu Peng sat with Lu You in the hotel lobby for more than an hour. Lu You had said to him afterward, “That assistant of yours is no simple kid. He knows too much about the company and about you.” He hadn’t taken it to heart at the time, had thought it was just Lu You saying something offhand. Thinking about it now, those words of Lu You’s might have weighed much more than he’d realized.

He’d thought he had climbed out of Diao Kexin’s pit. He’d come to Xinghuan, Wu You had given him a platform, given him authority, given him shares, and he’d turned his life around. He’d thought he was finally the man whose word went. But now he understood: he was still inside someone else’s game. Wu You gave him authority, gave him shares, gave him a two-million personal loan — and at the same time put his own nephew at his side. That wasn’t distrust; that was a boss’s instinct. If he’d been Wu You, he might well have done the same.

But it still left him choked up inside. He felt like someone who had just got out of the wolves’ den and walked into the tiger’s jaws without even noticing, and was still strutting around there like the big bad wolf. Diao Kexin had used him as a pawn, Gao Fei had used him as a pawn — and what did Wu You take him for now? A knife that came in handy, or a horse that needed a rein tied on it?

He sat there smoking one cigarette after another, until his throat was dry, until the Xi’an night outside the window had gone from deep black to gray-blue. He thought: Zheng Zhiyong, you’re just too green. You thought that going through one great disaster had made you mature, that you’d seen through people’s hearts. You haven’t. You’re still the same man who gets knocked senseless at the dinner table by a couple of nice words, still the same man who loses all sense of direction when someone praises him a little — “you’re so handsome,” “you’re so talented.”

He thought of Cong Shasha. That night at the hotel, when she bent down over him, something in his heart had let go. At the time he’d thought he hadn’t pushed firmly enough because of the drink. Thinking about it now, that wasn’t it. It was because he was greedy. Greedy for that bit of warmth, greedy for the feeling of someone coming close, greedy for that confirmation that “someone still wants me.” Cong Shasha had seen this clearly, just as Diao Kexin had seen it clearly back then.

He suddenly felt that Cong Shasha and Diao Kexin were really the same kind of person. It was only that Cong Shasha hadn’t been tempered to the right heat yet, hadn’t reached Diao Kexin’s level. But give it time? He remembered Cong Shasha saying to him, “What Ms. Diao can do, I’m not necessarily unable to do.” At the time it had sounded like a pledge of loyalty. Thinking back on it now, it was plainly a declaration.

Zheng Zhiyong stubbed out his cigarette, stood up and went to the window. The Xi’an sky was already light, and the man-made water features in the park gave off a cold gleam in the morning light. He thought: I can’t keep on like this. I have to pull my mind back — back onto the project, onto money, onto how to build Xinghuan up. Women, feelings, all that messy business — it all has to go on the back burner. If I fall flat one more time, I really won’t get up again.

As for this connection with Wu Peng, he wouldn’t say a word about it. Wu You hadn’t made it plain, Wu Peng hadn’t made it plain, so he’d act as if he didn’t know. But from now on, everything he said and everything he did in front of Wu Peng would have to pass through an extra sieve in his mind first. This man was a pair of eyes Wu You had put beside him. And he could use those eyes to let Wu You see what he wanted Wu You to see.
And the Sixth Academy business was even more trouble than Zheng Zhiyong had thought.

Half a month after the supplementary materials went in, the project office still said nothing about progress — said nothing about it being dead, either. It seemed simply to have stalled and stopped moving. Zheng Zhiyong called Supervisor Zhou twice, and each time Supervisor Zhou’s tone was more polite than the last — so polite, in the end, that Zheng Zhiyong understood: this wasn’t something Supervisor Zhou could decide.

He called Zhang Hailu into his office, shut the door and told him how things stood. Zhang Hailu heard him out, was silent for a while, then said, “Mr. Zheng, on this one we’ll have to find that top leader, Director Wu.”
Zheng Zhiyong said, “What if Old Wu is Yuanwang’s man?”
Zhang Hailu said, “Whether we do it this time or not, Yuanwang can’t do it anymore. Old Wu can’t change that either. And besides, we don’t even know whether he’s Yuanwang’s man.”

Zheng Zhiyong saw it all as clearly as a mirror. Back in the days when he and Diao Kexin were inseparable, Diao Kexin had lain in his arms on the phone with this Old Wu, in such a sweet, coquettish voice that he couldn’t help imagining whether something had already happened between the two of them. But as soon as Diao Kexin finished the call, she turned her body back toward him, her big eyes fluttering, buried her head in his chest and said, “Do you know how I get these old men to do things for us without them getting ideas about me?” Zheng Zhiyong said he didn’t. And Diao Kexin, in the tone of someone who had seen through all the coldness and fickleness of the world, said, “If you pay them enough, they can’t get ideas about me, can they? They can’t want the money and the woman both, can they?” And then she and Old Zheng were kissing, all tangled up together.

Back then Diao Kexin was Gao Fei’s lover, his sales director, the red thread that tied him to all his client resources — and more than that, the go-between for all his dirty deals. Looking back on it, even — for the sake of Gao Fei’s business, the hefty commissions and kickbacks, even the skimming off of the large sums paid out — was it possible she’d also been using her looks to keep those key client relationships going?
Zheng Zhiyong said, “We have to find a way to go meet this Director Wu.”
Zhang Hailu glanced at him and said in surprise, “How do we find him?”
Zheng Zhiyong said, “Song Li.”
Zhang Hailu said, “I don’t know if Song Li has that much pull. They’re in the same unit, but at different levels.”

The two of them asked Song Li on the spot. Song Li turned them down at once, saying there was too big a gap in rank between them and he didn’t have that kind of face — but he could introduce them to Director Wu’s confidant, Deputy Director Chen.

The dinner was set for two days later, at a private Huaiyang-cuisine restaurant near the Sixth Academy. The private room wasn’t big — one round table, just right for five or six. Song Li came along, and Deputy Director Chen; Zheng Zhiyong brought Zhang Hailu and Shasha. For the first half Old Zheng and Zhang Hailu kept talking about how solid their team was technically, how clear their advantages were — though the team hadn’t been put together long, its roots in the industry ran deep, and Shasha too had worked at Yuanwang all along and had dealt with the Sixth Academy for years.

Three rounds in, Deputy Director Chen put down his chopsticks, looked at Shasha and said, “Shasha, isn’t it? This isn’t the first time we’ve met, is it? We had dinner together over a year ago — do you remember? Back then you were at Yuanwang working under Ms. Diao, weren’t you?”

Only then did it dawn on Shasha. No wonder Deputy Director Chen had looked familiar when she came in; in a flash she remembered having had dinner with him and Director Wu. She said quickly, “Director Chen, of course I know! It’s just that I’ve only just changed places, so I was too embarrassed to say.”
Deputy Director Chen gave her a look and said, “Director Wu has a pretty good impression of you too.”

Shasha quickly raised her glass and toasted Deputy Director Chen, and said, “Oh my, then next time would it be all right for us to arrange something with Director Wu again? You see, we may be a new team, but we really are all old friends. Look, just like that the connection’s picked up again.”
Deputy Director Chen didn’t answer directly. He picked up his glass, drank the toast Shasha had offered, and said with a smile, “Shasha, you can ask Director Wu yourself. You don’t need me for that.”

Zheng Zhiyong watched Cong Shasha from beside her. Cong Shasha had come out of Yuanwang and followed Diao Kexin for seven years. At the dinner table she drew the eye too: twenty-eight, slim and straight-backed, more playful and lively than Diao Kexin, and when she got the chance to talk, poised and gracious too.
He glanced at Zhang Hailu. Zhang Hailu met his eyes, his face showing nothing, but Zheng Zhiyong knew he was thinking the same thing.

When the dinner broke up, Deputy Director Chen patted Zheng Zhiyong on the shoulder and said, “Mr. Zheng, I’d like to see this project of yours go through. Technically you really are strong. But some things — you know who to go to.” Then he looked at Shasha and said, “Shasha, this won’t do, you know. You can’t be so forgetful from now on.” Shasha took Director Chen’s hand. “I really didn’t forget you. It’s just that with all the leaders there, I was too shy to say much. Another day I’ll treat you on my own and make it up to you.” Deputy Director Chen, with the drink in him, held on to Shasha, and nodded, satisfied enough.

On the way back to the hotel, Zheng Zhiyong and Shasha sat side by side in the back of the car, not saying a word. Zhang Hailu sat in front and said nothing either. Halfway there, Zheng Zhiyong suddenly said, “Shasha, this is going to be up to you.”

Shasha answered, “At first I really had forgotten. Then I remembered — I’ve had dinner with Deputy Director Chen and Director Wu, had drinks with them, more than once. But every time, it was Ms. Diao who took Director Wu home, and when it came to keeping in touch with them afterward, she told me in no uncertain terms not to.”
Zheng Zhiyong said, “Have a look — do you have them on WeChat?”

Cong Shasha said, “I checked at dinner. I’ve got both of them on WeChat — added them more than a year ago. Apart from right at the start, when Director Wu sent me good-morning pictures in a group blast for ten days or so, we’ve never exchanged a single word.”

Zheng Zhiyong said, “Then why don’t you try asking him?” He remembered how Cong Shasha had looked that morning, sitting by the window in his shirt, looking at her phone; remembered her smile when she said, “What Ms. Diao can do, I’m not necessarily unable to do.” This request meant putting a woman who’d been with him into a very dangerous but very important position all over again. Thinking of what had happened between them that night, and of the price Shasha would have to pay next, Zheng Zhiyong felt a twinge of guilt.

The next day, by the time Zheng Zhiyong and Cong Shasha got back from Beijing to Xi’an it was already past five in the afternoon. They went straight from the airport to Old Zheng’s office, shut the door, and discussed it for a long time. “We have to get Director Wu on our side and find out what exactly the deal is between him and Diao. If we have to, we can outbid her.”
Cong Shasha was silent for a while, then said, “That’s what I was thinking too. You’ll need to get some things ready for me.”
Zheng Zhiyong said, “What things?”
Cong Shasha said, “Gold bars. Fifty-gram or hundred-gram gold bars.”
Zheng Zhiyong was silent for a while, then said, “Are you still in touch with Diao Kexin?”
Cong Shasha said, “No. We haven’t said a word to each other since I left.”
Zheng Zhiyong looked into her eyes. Cong Shasha looked back at him, without flinching. After a few seconds, Zheng Zhiyong said, “Do you know what it is you’re going to be doing?”
Cong Shasha said, “I know.”
Zheng Zhiyong said, “If you’ve never done this before, don’t wade into these muddy waters.”
Cong Shasha was taken aback for a moment, then said, “I’m the sales director. If I don’t go, who will?” What Cong Shasha was thinking was: how did Diao Kexin do it? She could do it too, for sure.
Zheng Zhiyong said, “All right, that’s enough for today. Are you hungry? I’ll order some takeout.”
Cong Shasha laughed. “I’m starving.”

When the takeout came, Old Zheng had ordered a very lavish meal. Cong Shasha said, “This takeout’s way too fancy — so many dishes. Let’s go up to your place on the fourth floor, where there’s a proper dining table.”

That was just what Old Zheng had in mind. The two of them went up together to Old Zheng’s dormitory on the fourth floor of the company. Dormitory, they called it, but really it was a very fine, luxuriously finished suite — and it was the first time Cong Shasha had come up to this floor of the office.

When the elevator doors opened, the corridor was so quiet she could hear the muffled thud of her own heels on the carpet. Zheng Zhiyong walked ahead, took out his key and opened the door. The moment it was pushed open, the first thing she noticed was a very faint woody scent, the kind of smell you’d only find in a hotel lobby — clean, cool, not like a place where anyone actually lived.

She went in, and the first thing she saw was the huge floor-to-ceiling window. The Xi’an night had already settled in; outside, the man-made water features glittered a little under the park’s streetlamps, and the footpaths and pavilions in the distance were pitch black, like a painting left unfinished. By the window stood an enormous freestanding bathtub, made of stone, strangely shaped. She didn’t recognize the brand, but she could tell it wasn’t cheap. Her heart gave a jolt — this didn’t look like the place of a man who’d just walked out on his ex-wife with nothing and owed a hundred thousand in debts.

Further in was a two-meter bed with dark gray bedding, made up neatly, the pillows set square, as if housekeeping had just tidied it. Between the bed and the sofa stood a slatted screen, and behind the screen was a wraparound sofa set. A few documents were spread on the coffee table, with an ashtray holding seven or eight cigarette butts, some stubbed out halfway, some burned down to the filter. Draped over the arm of the sofa was a navy blue outdoor jacket, one she’d seen him wear a few days before.

Against the wall was a whole wall of bookshelves, the books not very tidily arranged; a few had been pulled halfway out and pushed back in, as if someone had been reading and was called away by the phone. The rightmost section of the shelves, which she hadn’t noticed when she came in, she now saw was a hidden door, standing ajar, with a little light coming through. Zheng Zhiyong went over and pushed the hidden door open. Inside was a smaller room — a desk, a laptop, a desk lamp, and on the wall a schedule for the Sixth Academy project, several dates circled in red pen.

She stood at the floor-to-ceiling window looking out at the night, and suddenly thought of the little rented room back home in Xiangtan. It faced north and hardly saw the sun all year round; the plaster was peeling a bit on the walls, and she’d bought wallpaper herself and put it up, all crooked. She lived in that room for three years. When she left Yuanwang she handed the key back to the landlord, who refunded her 1,200 yuan deposit, and she took that money and had a bowl of rice noodles downstairs, then dragged her suitcase off to the high-speed rail station.

She turned her head and saw Zheng Zhiyong standing by the sideboard. He’d taken out a very exquisite set of tableware from the cabinet and was opening the takeout boxes one by one and turning them out into the fine dishes — six dishes and a soup — and setting them out very neatly at one end of a two-meter white marble dining table. He was very focused while he did it, as if afraid of spilling the soup, or afraid it wouldn’t look nice. She suddenly felt this man was a little pitiable. He lived in such a fine place, used such a fine bathtub, and this, though it was only takeout, had now been put into bone china that was obviously far from cheap — as if he were giving a girl like her, a stranger far from home, a dignified kind of care.

She glanced again at the two-meter bed, the dark gray bedding, the square-set pillows. She thought: Diao Kexin has never slept in this bed. What Diao Kexin slept in was that little one-bedroom he rented in Beijing, that office with dead fish floating in the tank, the back seat of that white BYD. This bed — she, Cong Shasha, was the first to walk in here.

The thought made that indescribable something in her heart slowly settle. She went over and sat down at the table and watched Zheng Zhiyong pour her red wine, watched him set chopsticks in front of her. She thought: what Ms. Diao can do, I’m not necessarily unable to do. But then she thought at once: I won’t be another Diao Kexin. Diao Kexin used men as ladders and threw them away once she’d climbed them. I won’t throw him away. I want to build this company up together with this man, and make it bigger than Yuanwang.

She raised her glass and clinked it against Zheng Zhiyong’s. The red wine swayed in the glass, rippling out a faint ring of light. She looked into his eyes and said, “Mr. Zheng, this is really lovely.”

At that vast white marble table, the two of them sat at one end, very close together. Old Zheng went to the wine cabinet and got another bottle of red, and they drank and refilled each other’s glasses. After a few rounds, Shasha gazed at Old Zheng with tears glistening in her eyes and said, “I don’t want to leave. Can I stay tonight?”
